Elon Musk reveals what really drives him to make humanity a star-faring civilization: “It’s life insurance, but for everything.” “If you simply look at the fossil record and look at how many extinction events have happened, which is a lot, then you know that this is simply a matter of time. It’s a when, not an if.” “It’s important to have insurance for life as a whole. It’s life insurance, but for everything.” But what motivates him even more: “I want to envision a future that’s exciting, that we’re out there exploring new frontiers, going to new star systems, and make science fiction not just fiction forever.” “We should boldly go like Star Trek, boldly go where no one’s gone before. And perhaps we find some long dead alien civilizations, or perhaps we find actual aliens we could talk to.” “You know how you can figure out if something’s really cool about the future? Just ask your kid, and they’ll tell you.” “Life cannot just be about solving one miserable problem after another. There have to be things that excite you and inspire you about the future, that make you happy when you wake up in the morning.” “You can’t wait to see what happens next. And being a star-faring civilization is one of those things.” Media

Elon Musk says SpaceX’s StarMind orbital AI satellite is a “much easier” engineering problem than Starlink V3: “I’m not sure why people think that making an AI satellite would be hard, given that SpaceX already has over 11,000 satellites in orbit, which is, I think, twice as much as the rest of the world combined.” “The StarMind satellite, which is the name for our overall compute system, is simpler, not harder than, say, the Starlink V3 communication satellite, which is an incredibly complex orbital radio station.” “It’s got the most advanced phased array antennas that have ever been made, far more advanced than anything that any military has at any price.” “Compared to that, the AI satellite is much, much easier, because it really just consists of a very large array of solar panels and a radiator.” “You’re gonna have about five times as much solar panel area as you will have radiator area. And that’s just basic physics.” “Then you have the star computer at the center, which would be physically about a quarter of the size of, say, a Vera Rubin NVL rack while having all of the capability of a Vera Rubin NVL72.” “I can’t emphasize enough that the StarMind satellite is a much easier technical problem than Starlink V3 communication satellite. Elon gave two talks today at DealBook and TomorrowX Summit, revealing more about SpaceX's plans than most earnings calls. Here are the 11 key takeaways: 1. SpaceX is scaling AI compute at an extraordinary pace: SpaceX is adding roughly 500 MW monthly, equivalent to 220,000 GB300s. Elon expects over 1 GW monthly by end-2027: a 6 GW annualized pace today, doubling to 12 GW. 2. Its build costs are far below industry estimates: Elon says outside estimates are off by up to 2x, with SpaceX building at roughly 60% of industry costs. Its in-house "Army X" builds the data centers, while Tesla Megapacks smooth training power. I'd already been modeling a 25–30% SpaceX cost advantage. 3. Anthropic could become a 10 GW customer: Anthropic told Elon its most likely outcome is renting another 10 GW from SpaceX, on top of existing capacity. Contracts allow termination with 3–6 months' notice, but Anthropic says staying is "extremely likely." This reinforces my model that Anthropic will take most upcoming capacity. 4. SpaceX is targeting a vastly larger telecom market: Elon argues AT&T and Verizon won't disappear as bandwidth demand explodes. Humans communicate at roughly 100 bits per second, while superintelligence and robots could require a trillion. SpaceX is targeting a market orders of magnitude larger than existing telecom revenue, as I'd modeled. Even more interestingly, this creates an opportunity to push its AI business further. 5. Its next-generation satellite network arrives next year: Direct to Cell V2 launches with 40x V1's bandwidth. Micro cell towers using 800 MHz and rooftop units resembling Starlink dishes will extend indoor coverage, with rooftop hardware entering production next year. Starlink is becoming a full scale carrier. 6. SpaceXSI has rebuilt its entire AI software stack: Over six to eight months, it rewrote training, reinforcement learning, and inference from scratch, close to the metal in C and C++. Elon thinks it "might have the best training stack software in the world." Grok 4.8 is also being built for practical usefulness rather than benchmark leadership, which is great for Grokbot. 7. Terafab could become the largest project on Earth: The facility is planned to reach 100 million square feet, with phase-one volume production targeted for late 2028. Elon says established chipmakers are risk-averse because of massive capex, while SpaceX will take risks and iterate rapidly toward a better chip process by 2028. 8. Optimus is moving toward industrial work: Elon expects an unstaged demonstration in a month or two and says Optimus could do dishes within 12–18 months. Its first major industrial role will be mining and refining ore for national security. 9. A Tesla–SpaceX merger is becoming increasingly logical: Elon says the companies are "probably" better together as AI and robotics bring them closer. Both have AI software teams and advanced chip-design capabilities, while superintelligence compute could eventually move into orbit. Shareholders will decide; Elon says he shouldn't receive an award simply for merging them. 10. Ship 42 could accelerate the entire Starship reuse program: Ship 42 needed only minor repairs before flying again, but SpaceX is retiring it for public display. This brings rapid reuse much closer. 11. SpaceX is targeting 200 GW of annual solar manufacturing for space: That's roughly 40% of average US electricity consumption. Its Starmind compute unit delivers the same capability at roughly a quarter the size of a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, which is a win in space. Elon says it's also simpler than Starlink V3, which is already in production. Simply put, SpaceX is building toward a trillion-dollar annual revenue business within just a few years, at scale never seen before. Many of these numbers I've already modeled and shared over the past few months. Yesterday's announcements bring those projections closer to reality. The scale of what's coming is extraordinary!

Great paper from Meta on ML engineering agents, tested with a large-scale A/B test on production search rankers. (bookmark it) They also show how important the harness design is. The agents propose a model change, implement it, train it, and evaluate it. Engineers keep control of the objective, the search direction, and the final review. In one campaign, the system completed 1,097 experiments and accepted 325 of them. That is a 29.6% acceptance rate, against 15.6% in an earlier campaign with a different objective. The best model raised search volume by 0.23% in the live test. They share that three problems made this hard. Each experiment takes hours, offline metrics often disagree with online impact, and gains flatten after the early wins. The team answered with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to online impact, and careful context engineering. Several accepted changes were architectures the team had never tried. The authors also report that a stronger model was not enough on its own. The loop around it mattered just as much. If you plan to put agents on your training pipeline, calibrate the objective first. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23910 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/mle-agents-autonomous-ml-engineering-in-large-scale-recommendation-systems-2611.23910

Banger paper from Google on self-improving agent harnesses. (bookmark it) It addresses common issues in self-improving agent harnesses like local overfitting, catastrophic forgetting, and memory pollution. They propose GUARD, which keeps the base model frozen and lets the agent edit its own prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. An edit is accepted only when its gains outweigh the behaviors it breaks. - On 43 hosted SDK tasks, GUARD reached 80.80% accuracy, 8.89 points over the starting harness (p = 0.008). - It beat Meta-Harness by 6.28 points and used 54.5% fewer tokens per task. - On procedural memory tasks, it led update correctness at 90.1% with zero memory pollution. Aggressive rewriters scored similarly and tripled pollution. How does it know what broke? Each task is split into self-checks before execution. Every round grades trajectories against them, pins rules the agent already handles, and ranks newly broken behaviors first. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23476 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/guard-stabilizing-recursive-self-improvement-with-regret-guidance-2611.23476

It can be almost 2000X faster than sklearn KMeans on select datasets and number of clusters. mlx-learn 0.1.5 is out, with OMeans: GPU clustering for Apple silicon, nearly 2,000× faster than scikit-learn's KMeans. 8,192 centroids on MNIST, on an M5 Ultra: scikit-learn KMeans: 191 s OMeans: 103 ms That is 1,854× faster, with held-out error within 0.1%. 1/8

It’s clear that agents need a different kind of cloud. They run for hours, wait on people, and run code they wrote themselves. Volcano brings sandboxes, durable workflows, Postgres, and hosting into one platform, so coding agents can build and deploy on it. At Kong we run half a quadrillion AI tokens a year, and I kept seeing agents stuck on clouds built for websites. So we built a cloud for agents. Volcano is live today: the self-healing agent cloud. Sandboxes, durable workflows, Postgres, hosting.

“Worth a look?” was the last line of the sponsorship email I sent to 11 people. The sentence before it is the one I’d use again. I typed my request in Claude, and @lemlist drafted a four-step email sequence for my sponsorship list. When I opened the first email in lemlist, the offer and “Worth a look?” were already there, one right after the other. I kept both. I sent just the first email. The subject line was “[Company] + the ecommerce operators I write for.” In the email, I got more specific about who reads my newsletter: people who run email and retention at Shopify stores. I included my LinkedIn and X audience numbers too, but if you sell software to those teams, knowing who reads the newsletter tells you more about fit than my follower count does. Then came the offer: “If you have a push coming in Q1, I can send the sponsorship sheet with placements and rates.” One of the 11 people I emailed said they’d take a look at the sheet, so I sent it over the next morning. They had my placements and rates without having to book a call.
